title: When Bias Meets Trainability: Connecting Theories of Initialization
claim: As a control parameter increases, the system shifts from a neutral state to a polarized one, passing through a uniform critical point.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, each with an inset histogram above a density plot
description: Three side-by-side line plots share a y-axis labeled p_y(L) and an x-axis labeled y(L). The panels are titled γ(L) = 0.05, 1.0 and 10.0. Each panel has two Gaussian curves, blue for class 1 and red for class 2. At γ = 0.05 the curves almost coincide and are centered near zero. At γ = 1.0 they are partly separated, with moderate overlap. At γ = 10 they are fully separated into two distant bumps. Above each density plot is a small gray inset histogram of p_g0 over g0 from 0 to 1. The insets change from a bell shape centered at 0.5, to a flat uniform shape, to a U shape with peaks at both ends. A legend sits between the first two panels. The eye goes first to the Gaussian curves, then to the insets.
caption: Example of pre-activation distributions for neutrality (left) and moderate prejudice (right) computed by sampling Gaussian variables with synthetic data. The inset plots show the distribution of the dataset elements classified into the reference class G0. In the neutral phase, G0 is centred around 0.5, while with moderate prejudice, G0 concentrates at the extremes. At the transition between these two phases, G0 is uniformly distributed (middle).
abstract: The statistical properties of deep neural networks (DNNs) at initialization play an important role to comprehend their trainability and the intrinsic architectural biases they possess before data exposure Well established mean field (MF) theories have uncovered that the distribution of parameters of randomly initialized networks strongly influences the behavior of the gradients, dictating whether they explode or vanish. Recent work has showed that untrained DNNs also manifest an initial guessing bias (IGB), in which large regions of the input space are assigned to a single class. In this work, we provide a theoretical proof that links IGB to previous MF theories for a vast class of DNNs, showing that efficient learning is tightly connected to a network prejudice towards a specific class. This connection leads to a counterintuitive conclusion: the initialization that optimizes trainability is systematically biased rather than neutral.
